utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Coo. If I could remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Coo.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Let me try that again. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Coo. Do you hear me loud and clear? As we broke yesterday I was attempting to put a page of your testimony in the Milosevic case, which I'm rather hoping you might have before you now but I may be wrong. 10094, we were looking for.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's on its way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have it there or is it still --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It still seems to be missing from my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I am so sorry. We have it in the process of being copied. I think that's -- let me move on until it comes back to us. And if I could turn then -- do you have 10103?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good. I had asked you yesterday about your concerns in relation to the arming of the civilian population and as your testimony was there you made this observation, that "there are risks or dangers inherent in arming one ethnic group and disarming another ethnic group when those ethnic groups are mutually hostile." And let me take you also 10104 at line 3. Again, you said, I was pointing out that there was a mutual hostility between the Serbian ethnic groups and the Albanian, or elements of the Albanian ethnic group. And to arm one and disarm the other had risks." Were you there commenting in your analysis that the policy of seeking to disarm Kosovan Albanians and to arm the civilian populations of Serb and other non-Albanian ethnic minorities was a negative move as far as the Serb authorities were concerned?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at most all I could say that [sic] it was a risky move, given the mutual hostility of the two groups. It may have been necessary from their perspective, but it had risks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, just take an example that is perhaps closer to my home than yours at least. If you can imagine, for instance, in the early 1970s if the Unionist government in northern Ireland had armed all the Protestants and disarmed all the Catholics, that is not something you would have thought of as being a very smart move.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't. And the situation with local defence in Kosovo is that they were supposed to be part of an official chain of command and trained. And in theory, they should have been disciplined or had some semblance of discipline. Whether they did or not, I can't really say, but that's one difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I really am having problems understanding your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, if it helps, I didn't have any trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It would, certainly, Your Honour. It's maybe that I'm not wearing earphones, so I'm having difficulty hearing the witness. As I read it it makes more sense than it was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think it would be very helpful to explore the examples of other problems, because there are so many distracting elements. It would be better to concentrate on the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I will come back to rogue elements rather than distracting ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The state of emergency I want to move to now which at page 36 of yesterday's transcript at line 12 you said that in April -- already by April 1998 "the chief of the General Staff... felt that the situation was sufficiently drastic that it warranted the declaration of a state of emergency." Is that still your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You see -- can we just look at tab 9, which is the document that you were referring to there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You have that page 03055099?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Last paragraph on that page 1A, the situation -- this is the letter of course to Mr. Milosevic that had been written by General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And he is drawing to Milosevic's attention a number of negative facts which he numbers 1 through 6 just above that paragraph. Yes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: He itemises these, and I'm not going to go through all of them, but there are issues that I'd like to address with you. Firstly, the constant tendency to use the Yugoslav army outside the system's institutions. And when he itemises what he means by that, he says to Mr. Milosevic, 1A, "the situation in Kosovo could have been overcome if a state of emergency had been declared in time on the 20th of April, 1998, when I sent you a proposal in writing." I don't think we have that proposal. Have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen the proposal, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And he continues. "Since you did not accept it, the situation has escalated and MUP representatives and you yourself have asked that the Yugoslav army be deployed. Some small units were directly and indirectly deployed, which is illegal from the point of view of the law, while the repercussions for the state are well-known." Now, what I want to ask you on that is of course the only way that he could use the army legally, other than at the border area to secure the borders of the state, was by the declaration of a state of emergency, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- that's been a common interpretation of the Serb constitution and law, and whether that's accurate or not I can't say because I'm not an expert on the FRY law. But it certainly appears that the constitution and the law had provisions for use of the army in internal security operations that required the declaration of an extraordinary state.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You really couldn't just say "yes" in answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't because the constitution isn't clear enough to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Okay. So if other forces -- sorry, if the army were to be used anywhere else, it was necessary to declare a state of emergency. That's what it comes down to, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it comes down to in some people's interpretation of the constitution, and in particular in this instance General Perisic's. And I presume he has a better understanding of what is legal and what isn't legal than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In your careful researches into the operations of and the command structure of the Yugoslav army, have you encountered contrary interpretations?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't research this point in depth because that was outside my expertise. It would be delving into interpretations of the Serbian -- the FRY constitution and FRY law which I have no expertise in. I've heard from some witnesses that this wasn't illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Have you sought legal expertise on this point from the substantial staff available to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the Prosecution in the Milosevic case have. That wasn't part of my mandate as far as my support to that case went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So are you saying you do not know what the answer to the question is?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Continue over the page, please, at point B. General Perisic is saying: "In order to implement the conclusions from the session of the VSO command council -- supreme command council of the 9th of June, 1998, we requested the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to ensure the legal conditions." So therefore we have the supreme command council of the army is asking the government to ensure the legal conditions, namely the proclamation of one of the following: A state of emergency or an imminent threat of war and material and financial conditions, which he's also sent an attachment obviously requesting. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has still not done this, so there's been no movement since April of 1998, and this is now the 23rd of July, 1998. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Which means that every act of engagement by the VJ in combat operations outside the border area continues to be unlawful and the potential repercussions are unforeseeable. Again with the caveat that you don't know whether it's unlawful or not, this is the general's advice to his president. Right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Now, outside the border area you would understand to include, among other places, Lapusnik. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Decani, Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm going to go on down to point 3 on that page where he highlights the fact that, as it appeared to him on the 23rd of July, 1998, people who were not members of the army were attempting to command army units. You see that point?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: He refers to constant aspirations by members of the MUP to have some VJA/VJ units supported to them -- excuse me, subordinated to them, this leads to misunderstandings if the units are not given. And if they are given this respects unauthorised and unprofessional use which has counter-effects, the best examples being Decani and Orahovac, is written there, the Serb names.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In other words, what he's highlighting there was the appalling massacres that had taken place in those locations as being a direct result of unauthorised persons commanding army units. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree with that. It's not clear in his --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, what do you understand him to mean by -- naming those two particular locations?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar enough with what happened at those locations at that time. He could very well simply be referring to the use of the VJ outside its proper chain of command. I can't extend that interpretation to include allegations by General Perisic that atrocities had been committed by the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, are you completely unaware of atrocities having been committed at those locations?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the detail -- I'm not aware of the details. I'm aware of allegations that atrocities were committed at numerous locations in Kosovo by both sides. I didn't make a particular study of these two incidents, particularly 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I want to give you an opportunity to reconsider the frankness of that answer, Mr. Coo. You are aware, are you not, that it is at least alleged that an appalling massacre took place in Drenica in March, March the 9th of 1998. The Jashari family. You've heard of that, have you not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Right. You are area that an appalling massacre is said to have taken place at Rahovec, also that year, are you not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard that one did. I haven't seen any details on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, we recognise that you've been frank enough to say that there are limitations to your expertise. But as you look at that line in the third paragraph of the general's letter, what other possible interpretation do you think is to be put on that other than references to massacres by Serbs? Is this so hard for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said earlier, Your Honours, the other interpretation is that this is -- General Perisic is pointing out that he had a problem with the illegal use of the VJ, the use of the VJ in internal security operations without a declaration of the state of emergency. There's -- as far as I'm aware, the VJ's involvement in the Prekaz massacre is unclear and I've never been asked to look at that massacre in detail. From my report for this case I was never asked to look at the details of any operations or to determine whether or not the VJ had been involved in massacres. So I can't say from that paragraph what General Perisic is complaining about specifically. I think it would be an unreasonable leap to make to assume that he's talking about Prekaz and Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Oh, you remember the name Prekaz now do we?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've always remembered that name, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Splendid. That's an unreasonable leap. Very well. He refers at B to attempts by civilian members of the staff to command the corps, and he continues over the page by pointing out that operations had been planned with -- in cooperation with civilian members of the staff and reported to Sainovic and Minic. Sainovic was who?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a federal deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: For what area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what his specific function was in the government, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but he was assigned to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: He was assigned to Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And who was Minic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minic was another SPS official who was assigned to Kosovo by Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: President of the Assembly, was he not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And those two were distributing tasks to everyone except the Pristina Corps. And in practice the commander of the Pristina Corps plans what he is ordered to do, which is at the request of Sainovic, Minic, and the MUP. So again, we have a military chain of command that is being totally subverted by nonmilitary personnel; that appears to be the complaint of General Perisic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one aspect of General Perisic's complaint, Your Honours. The chain wasn't completely subverted. As many of the VJ documents show, they were still reporting up their chain of command, Pristina Corps reporting to the 3rd army, the 3rd army reporting to the General Staff, and tasks being sent down through the 3rd army to the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The army still had some control over the army. I'm not suggesting otherwise. The problem is armies are not supposed to be run, even in part, by civilians, are they? You know that.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not quite true. The supreme commander of the army was President Milosevic. The joint command was established by him to coordinate operations in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Is that your best answer? You know what I'm talking about. I'm talking about the operational command of army units. Mr. Coo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way the joint command seems to have worked from the documents we have on the joint command, Your Honours, was that the civilian membership of the joint command were there to ensure that the objectives of President Milosevic were achieved in Kosovo. They did this by meeting with the -- among others, the MUP leadership and the VJ leadership in Kosovo. Those commanders, the MUP and the VJ commanders, were the technical experts on the deployment of the VJ and the MUP in Kosovo. They presented -- they were -- Milosevic's aims were relayed to them through the joint command, sometimes by Milosevic. Those aims were interpreted by the VJ and the MUP and eventually became orders. The orders -- the planning and the ordering was done by the MUP and the VJ chains of command. The direction, strategic direction, was being provided by the civilian members of the joint command, but they did not have the technical training to actually command and direct the implementation of -- or the undertaking of military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm really struggling to understand you here, Mr. Coo. Are you seeking to be a wholesale apologist for the way the VJ conducted its affairs and saying essentially that General Perisic 's concerns were completely unfounded and that everything was done in a proper military fashion? That's the impression I'm getting. I may be the only one in the room with that impression, but help me.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly not the impression I'm trying to give, Your Honours. I'm trying to explain how the armed Serb operations were tasked and operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Was there a difference between how they were meant to function and how they were functioning, from your studies as an expert on military analysis?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was with the imposition of the joint command in Kosovo. That joint command -- there were no provisions that I could find in any legislation for a joint command, but there's equally nothing to stop the president from going through the proper procedures to set up a joint command as was done in 2001. And as an example of this elsewhere, the equivalent existed at least at one point in Northern Ireland. It's ensuring that there's civilian oversight of a complicated -- politically complicated issue. Whether Milosevic went through the proper procedures to do this, it appears that he probably didn't. But if I was to be asked to establish conclusively whether laws were violated or the constitution violated, I couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Of course you couldn't establish that conclusively, and I'm not suggesting that you should be able to. I shall resist the temptation to visit Northern Ireland again, but I would ask you to come with me this far, Mr. Coo, in agreeing that General Perisic was raising some extremely important questions from any military point of view. Would you not agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Fine. Then perhaps we can move on. You expressed your concern in the Milosevic trial about the failure by the VJ to investigate apparent violations or alleged violations of international humanitarian law amongst its own staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: There appeared, as far as you were aware from your extensive studies of the documentation, to be no indication that anybody on the VJ side had been investigated, particularly from the standpoint of the command responsibility for violations of international humanitarian law. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you were highly critical of that failure.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I pointed this out. I wouldn't say I was critical.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You wouldn't regard that as a point of criticism?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a criticism, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, okay. You were also critical, I suggest, of the facts that those who had been in command-responsibility positions at the time when violations of international humanitarian law appeared to be -- have been committed under their command was subsequently promoted to higher positions. You found that a cause for concern. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Indeed, at one point in your testimony you noted that the VJ's book from 2001 -- what book were you referring to there, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a book published by the VJ publishing house in 2001. I don't remember the full title, but it had to do with whether or not the VJ adhered to the -- to international humanitarian law in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: That was essentially a book brought out by the VJ aimed at demonstrating that it had, by and large at least, adhered to international humanitarian law, about which of course opinions may differ, but that was the purpose of the book.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem that that's what it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And that book did indicate - and you pointed this out in your testimony - that mass graves had been found, that crimes had been committed, but that no investigations had taken place into those with command responsibility. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Have you -- turning for a moment to MUP. Have you seen evidence that those responsible for commanding MUP units were responsible for financial expenditure outside the law? And I use a phrase used by General Perisic in his complaint to Mr. Milosevic: "financial expenditure outside the law by those responsible for commanding MUP units." Have you seen any evidence of that sort?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't. No, I didn't look into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you look into the operations of MUP in Ferizaj, for instance?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No. Has anyone asked you to ignore concerns of that sort?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never been asked to ignore anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You would agree, would you not, that from much of the material that you have presented in your various tabs to the Tribunal, there was a consistent media propaganda campaign in the Serb media against the KLA calling in terms for the liquidation of each and every member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an anti-KLA propaganda or an anti-KLA message in the media. I don't specifically recall calls for liquidation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Politika, p-o-l-i-t-i-k-a, was a Serb state-run newspaper. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Would you look up tab 42 for us for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just point out for the record, tab 42 is one of the additional documents that I submitted yesterday. It was not part of the body or supporting material of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. P237 I understand is the -- thank you very much - reference there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you want the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: P237 I understand is the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And I'm looking at the second page of that exhibit R025-1458. And do you see at 3.11, go to the very bottom of that paragraph, you see the word "Politika." Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: This would appear to refer to an article in the state-run paper quoting the Serbian Radical Party. "It is necessary to exterminate Albanian terrorists." And if you look just down, a little bit below that, SRS issued a press statement indicating that "it demands that the competent state authorities of the Republic of Serbia as well as the VJ resort to a fierce action so as to exterminate and liquidate Albanian terrorist gangs and prevent the infiltration -- armed Albanian gangs from Albania." It goes on in like terms. Just using that as one example you will recall that throughout the media reports cited in the various ECMM documents that you've referred to, there is a universal use of the word "terrorist" always to -- accompanying the word "Albanian." Would you agree with that as well?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So we have an atmosphere, would you agree, in which the constant propaganda to which the armed forces occupying Kosovo were subject, assuming they read newspapers, referred constantly in derogatory terms to Kosovar Albanians. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the very limited media information I've read, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And would you also agree from your reading of the extensive documentation that we have from the various generals and other military commanders that are annexed to your report, that there is a constant use of the word "Siptar" to describe Kosovar Albanians? Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a common word, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you are aware that not only is it common, it is recorded by Kosovan Albanians as a highly derogatory term?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I've seen is that in the translations we get from our translation service is that they put "derogatory" in brackets beside it. I've also heard people say that it's actually not that derogatory. So I can't really say if it is or not. I don't know how the Kosovar Albanians regard that term. I've never asked one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You are aware at the very least that there is controversy at the use of that term. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And again if I can make a very quick excursion to Northern Ireland for one brief minute, you would agree that it would be wholly inappropriate for a British general stationed in northern Ireland to be writing to his subordinates or his superiors about Paddies or Micks.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It's not in other words -- the word "Siptar" is not something you think appropriate, if there is a derogatory interpretation, to be used by someone of the rank of general?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd agree, if it is a derogatory term.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move with you to the KLA itself and of course immediately -- please understand that I accept your statement yesterday that you have never been asked to review the command structure of the KLA and that therefore I assume you've never seen any specific evidence that the KLA had any command structure in the conventional military sense, as you understand a command structure to be. Am I right in that assumption?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read some documents that describe the structure of the KLA, including the General Staff, the zone system, the brigades. I haven't made a point of studying it, so I can't really comment as an expert on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Maybe you can tell us what documents you have read.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read the Human Rights Watch book on Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Is there a description of the command structure of the KLA in that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is, to my recollection. The -- I've also read - and I don't remember the specific documents - but there have been some internal documents in the OTP produced on the structure of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, if there are any of those that you think might be helpful to us, I am sure you will find a way of getting them to us. Now, did you hear or read the evidence of Colonel Crosland to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm generally aware of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No, my question was did you hear or read it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read some of it, yes. And I heard some of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It only lasted two days, but you've heard and read some of it. Would you agree that Colonel Crosland, who is obviously a man of considerable military experience and considerable -- well, let's stop there, considerable military experience. Yes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: That he has, by comparison with most at least, considerable on-the-ground experience of Kosovo at the material time, the time material to this case?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And would you in general terms be inclined therefore to defer to his views and his experience? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Indeed is there any specific way in which you would disagree with what you have heard or what you have read about his testimony to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing specific that I can think of at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, is there anything generally?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing generally I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Okay. Nothing generally, nothing specific. Therefore I assume nothing. I think you have already accepted that KLA communiques, some of which you have exhibited, were essentially PR documents. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was probably their main function. What I derived from them was descriptions of some of the operations that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Their primary purpose being to boost morale within the KLA. Yes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect that was a purpose, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And also to trumpet the strength of the KLA to the wider world?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And of course there is a considerable risk, is there not, in accepting documents that have that purpose at their face value?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is, and I at no point accepted them at face value.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And I thought we were clear on that. Certainly those communiques do not constitute anything that you would regard as military orders of the type that you would expect to see emanating from the high command of an army?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they're not orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No. Looking at the issue of military command structure, would you agree that -- with the following as a reasonable definition of military command: "One, the ability to give and follow orders in a command framework where there is some system with an established legal or lawful basis to ensure that these orders will be obeyed." Would you agree with that -- that part of that definition of military command? I'm not saying it's exhaustive, but would you agree that that is partial definition?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a partial definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Would you agree further that there should also be some system of lawfully removing someone from command if other commanders recognise that their orders are not being obeyed or are not lawful?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. You can command a military or a military-type unit without a legal basis. You can remove people from units without being backed up by a law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, for a command structure, there presumably has to be some system of removing someone from command. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there should be a system; whether it's legally based or not is a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And when we talk about a system, a command structure, whether it's within the law of the country in which its operating or not, it has to have its own internal law in order to be understood and to have effect. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think internal regulations. I don't think militaries can necessarily set established laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Fine. Internal regulations I'm quite comfortable with. And that these have to be clearly understood or understandable to those who are required to give and receive those orders?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Have you come across anywhere any evidence that any person in the KLA demonstrated this command capacity during the time frame of this indictment?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't, but I haven't looked at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree that the mere fact that a group calls itself an army doesn't necessarily give it the standing of an army in traditional military terms?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Would you agree that the fact that that army promulgates a rule book doesn't necessarily imply that there is the authority to enforce those rules?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In your own testimony in Milosevic you laid emphasis on the importance of continuity of command, meaning both the reporting upwards chain of command and also you gave as an example the importance of ensuring measures to address the possibility of a commander being killed in action or otherwise placed incapacitated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Page reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I was afraid you were going to ask for that, and give me a moment, please. It's one that I did have flagged. Will you allow me to come back to you on that, please? First of all, could I ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Coo, giving that as your evidence that there has to be an upwards and downwards chain of command?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember saying that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And also the importance of ensuring that there is a basis for replacing a commander who is either killed or placed hors de combat?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, was there an answer?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Would you look for a second at tab 43. What number that? Do we know? P238 I'm told. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: If you just turn to the second page, R0251452. And if you look under Kosovo at the bottom, Regional Items, Kosovo. Point 5. Pec. TM, that's the mobile team, is it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Visited -- or it might be an individual. I'm not sure. Anyway, "visited the UCK village of" -- I'm sorry, I can't read it. Anyway it's a small village, "population 4318, and met with the recently elected military UCK leader of the village." Now, how many armies in your experience elect their commanders?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any that do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: What we're dealing with here essentially, would you agree, appears to be a group of villagers who've said to one of their number, Would you mind taking charge? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. That's one implication, but it's sufficiently vague that it -- it's not clear what procedures they went through precisely to appoint him to that position. They use the term "elected," but how they did it I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The point makes itself. I'm grateful. I'm told the page reference that I had been seeking was 9988. And yes, lines 1 through 14 detail what you -- what you were saying is important in relation to continuity in military operations. If you just want to peruse that quickly and make sure I haven't misstated that in any way.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd still agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. You may recall from what you heard or read of Colonel Crosland's evidence that he several times made the point that in the time frame we are considering, the KLA was essentially very much a fledgling movement. Have you seen anything that causes you to disagree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really comment on that. I don't know enough about the background or the setup of the KLA to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: That's fair enough. He gave his opinion on what he believed the Serb thought process was at the time, and the reference to this - I'm afraid I don't have copies available - is at Day 19 -- excuse me, yes, Day 19, pages 57 through 58. In the context of control by the Serbs and the attempts to exercise control he said that the Serb thought process was: "We'll blitzkrieg the area and drive the civilian population out of it in and attempt to try and control or militarily control the area by fear rather than by any proper strategic thought." Now, would you first of all agree that that appeared to be the mind-set or the modus operandi of the VJ and MUP forces in such of their campaign in 1998, from the documents you've seen?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that one outcome of the operations conducted by the VJ and MUP was the civilian population being driven out and military control made easier to establish as a result. But whether there was any absence -- whether there was any strategic thought or not I can't say. I think that although -- although I should remark that the summer offensive, the establishment of the joint command and the organisation required to conduct the summer offensive in 1998 had to involvement a great deal of strategic thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Now, as far as the numbers of the KLA in the time frame that we're considering, as far as they're concerned -- could we have a look at tab 10, please. This is the letter by General Pavkovic to the commander of the 3rd army in which he asserts that - and I'm looking at the first page, point 1, the fourth paragraph, the third line - he says: "The terrorist organisation has managed in a relatively short time to mobilise respectable forces, numbering at this time 3.500 and 4.500 men, armed and trained for armed raids and guerrilla operations." Now, that is a letter dated the 13th of May, 1998. If we could go to your report at paragraph 45. You see three lines from the bottom -- do you have that -- sorry, paragraph 45. It's page 14 of your report.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You have that there. "By mid-May about 5.000 VJ personnel had been assigned to the conflict against -- an estimated KLA strength of 3.500 to 4.500." And you reference that document. Now, you appear to accept that unquestioningly. Why is that, Mr. Coo, that figure of 3.500 to 4.500?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it's accepted unquestioningly. I put in "estimated." The purpose of this -- the focus of this was more on the strength of the VJ, but I believe that the VJ would have come to that figure from its own intelligence and I've got no basis to counter it. I can't really agree with it or disagree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: But you state it as fact, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to that. The fact stated is that the VJ in the document estimated the force of that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, as I read that, you say as fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think there's any point in debating the argument about what is thought or not thought from there. What is stated can be put to the witness and his comments received on it, and I think there will be no difficulty at all in that being done, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I think I can just about manage that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: This is a figure that you have not cross-checked with any other analysis. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen other figures and, for example, I'm aware of Colonel Crosland's much lower figure. All I can say is that the KLA would have had to have had a sizeable force to be able to gain control and retain control of 30 per cent of the Kosovo territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, you're jumping ahead of me, but I'll catch up with you, don't worry. You would agree as a matter of military history and experience that a small guerrilla force in -- particularly in mountainous or difficult territory can hold down a very, very substantial army and prevent that army from exercising its own control or make it at least extremely difficult. You would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. The force ratios for insurgent forces are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And I don't know if you recall Colonel Crosland's testimony that having gone with KLA members from Rahovec to Malisevo, his estimate of their numbers was so low that he considered he could take them out with 50 good men. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, and I now recall that that's one area where I questioned his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: He was there; you weren't. On what basis do you question his testimony?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to know is the -- what he's considering the KLA to comprise when he quotes that figure, whether that -- whether he's including the village-defence aspect of the KLA or whether he's just considering simply the full-time cadre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: All right. Then are you aware of General Wesley Clark's testimony in the Milosevic case? Did you review that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of it; I didn't review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Maybe that can be made available to all the parties. It's 30389 -- or do I have those? I think I probably have those.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher -- I think the -- the interpreters need copies. Thank you. I'm sorry. I thought we had enough. While we're waiting, just if you have a look at pages 3, 4, 5, and 6, those will be the ones most relevant to what we're going to discuss. The interpreters now have copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Look first of all at General Wesley Clark's testimony 30389, lines 1 through 16. This concerned his meeting in October 1998 with General Djordjevic. If you bear that date in mind, would you, October 1998. "Q. In the course of your discussion with Djordjevic and in the marking of the map, was it possible to count the number of alleged KLA people concerning Djordjevic? "A. Yes, we added up these numbers and they totalled 410 KLA, according to Djordjevic's analysis." Let me just ask you this: Who was General Djordjevic in October of 1998?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Djordjevic was the head of the public security sector of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: "Q. Did you raise that with him; and if so tell us what he said. "A. Well, I certainly did. I said that you've forced -- words to the effect you've forced 350.000, 400.000 people out of their homes; Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you're trying to destroy the province to get at 400 people. He said, 'we were within two weeks of killing them all. Why did you stop us?' And I said, 'because you're targeting a civilian population and it's creating a humanitarian catastrophe for your own people.'" Now, that figure, the 410, was that something you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only through General Wesley Clark's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you double-check that with MUP sources?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was never a requirement to. I was looking at 1999 primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Okay. Over the page we have Lord Paddy Ashdown's visit in late September of 1998. And here he is being cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic. And he's giving his views, and I'm putting this to you so that you can give us yours when you've heard this. At line 1, page 2440. "Mr. Milosevic, it may help if I were able to explain that my view at the time was that there were, in effect, three KLAs. There was a KLA which was a village defence force, little more. I suspect that Mr. Rugova did have effectively control - and this is an opinion, no more - over what you might call the Home Guard elements of the KLA. I suspect that this was predominantly the case in rural areas." Let me pause there. Does the expression "Home Guard elements" carry any recognition to you or is that an English term?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And what does it mean to you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's essentially a local defence concept, units that are responsible primarily for defending their immediate area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's continue. "There was a second KLA, which was probably the KLA which I saw more clearly in the Bajram Curri area, probably much better organised politically, over whom, in my view, if Mr. Rugova had control, it was a diminishing control; if you like, the radicalised KLA. "Then there was a third KLA, which was known as FARK - and I have no doubt you're aware of them - who were of a different political persuasion, and the control lines from them, it seemed to me, ran back to Mr. Sali Berisha." So -- let me just finish it off then. "Now, if you -- those are opinions, judgements. I can't prove any of them, but that was what I said. And in my view, Mr. Rugova had a good control over the LDK elements in the countryside and therefore of the Home Guard elements of the KLA. We used 'KLA' as a - I'm sure you did too - as a sort of umbrella term within which, I think, several organisations lived." Now again, reminding you he's talking substantially there of a visit in late September 1998. Were you, first of all, aware of Lord Ashdown's theory that there were more than one KLAs in operation?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, from his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And again, have you seen any reason to disagree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I haven't looked at this, so I haven't seen any documents that would allow me to disagree. I would only say that Lord Ashdown was in Kosovo for a very brief tour. I presume he got most of his information from Colonel Crosland on the KLA structure. How many of it he remembered, I don't know, but clearly he remembered some. His description of it broken down into these elements don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: But again --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- mean that there weren't some command and control links between the different elements; he hasn't ruled that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Neither has he ruled it in?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Essentially again, I think you're recognising that the expert in this field is Colonel Crosland rather than yourself?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland does know more about the KLA structure than I do. If I could just comment, Your Honours, on General Clark's testimony briefly. There's one caution I would like to throw in. This discussion took place with General Djordjevic in 1998 which was after the summer offensive when it seems that the VJ - and this is corroborated by a KLA communique which is in my report - the VJ and the MUP were successful in largely crushing the KLA. So I have to wonder whether the 410 KLA marked on the map in October of 1998 was the current size of the KLA and not the size during the summer offensive. I can't say that for certain, but that's just a concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that the Serb offensive must have resulted in wiping out 3.000 to 4.000 KLA members between May of 1998 and October of 1998. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The VJ/MUP offensive seems to have been deemed a success, and the KLA communique in August 1998 where they describe their tactical retreat I think it, was tends to support that. I don't know how many were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: May I just remind you, in case we all lose sight of it, that your report to this Tribunal at page 1 of that report says under the heading "Scope of the Report," "this report examines the nature of the armed conflict in Kosovo during the first eight months of 1998." Isn't it the fact from what you're saying that that's the last thing it does?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary. It certainly isn't an examination or a blow-by-blow account of the conflict between the KLA and the MUP forces because I didn't -- the Serb forces because I didn't have that information at hand. But it is one description using a variety of sources of what took place in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of Lord Ashdown's description of the KLA's positions as "very rudimentary, pathetically prepared military positions, all the signs of people who have got or have had no military training"?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that comment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Would you disagree with it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say because I haven't looked at that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: See, you've described your expert report to this Tribunal as - and I'm looking at the screen now - "one description using a variety of sources of what took place in Kosovo." Would you agree that your description is based on a very selective variety of sources?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's based on certain sources and I wasn't able to consider witness testimony such as General Ashdown -- Lord Ashdown's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're full-time employed here. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You have been the head of MAT since when?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since August 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Since August?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. You have 18 people working under you. Yes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You filed your report or analysis on the 2nd of August, 2004, in this case. Yes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Since that date have you kept under review any questions that may have arisen in this or any other case that might affect the validity or content of any aspect of this report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't been able to follow this case closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. Have you kept under review any questions that may have arisen in this or any other case that might affect the validity or content of any aspect of this report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. That hasn't been a specific function.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Before coming here yesterday to testify, did you spend any time at all in preparation of your testimony with counsel for OTP?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: How much time did you spend?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: That was just with counsel?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Aside from spending approximately three hours with counsel, did you take time on your own to review the report yourself?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In doing so, did it occur to you to check to see whether any items or matters of concern that might affect your report may have arisen since you wrote that report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened to most of Colonel Crosland's testimony because I thought that would be most relevant to the report, since I understood that he would have the best insight into the conflict at that time. In addition, I continued my function as an analyst on Kosovo and I was working primarily on the Serb cases, but in that process I look at a lot of documents and any new documents that come in. And if any had affected the Limaj report, I would have amended the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do I assume from that last answer that there were no documents that came to your attention working on any of the Serb cases which affected your report in this case?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, I've asked you so far about your efforts to check matters that have arisen since your report on 2nd of August last year. In writing your report did you take into consideration what your own testimony had been in September of 2002 --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: -- in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you take into consideration what Colonel Crosland's testimony had been in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read his Milosevic testimony, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you find it uninteresting, irrelevant, unreliable?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Is there any reason why you haven't made any reference to his expertise in this field in your report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I intentionally did not include witness testimony or witness statements in my report. As was done in my Milosevic report; in that case the Trial Chamber rejected all references to witness testimony. And as military analysts we prefer not to rely on witness testimony. Our reports are written primarily on documentary evidence. I was also asked by the trial team for this case not to include witness testimony in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Were you asked by the trial team in this case not to speak to any experts in this field?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Would that not be a normal thing for you to do as a military analyst preparing an expert report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any experts with whom I could have spoken with about this. So the limitations in my report, the scope of my report, is quite clear I think. I relied on roughly four categories of documents to describe some aspects of the armed conflict in 1998. I couldn't reach any conclusive opinions on how the -- how the armed conflict unfolded in detail, for instance on how many men the KLA lost, how many men the Serb forces lost, or where specifically the front lines were, and what sort of bunkers the KLA set up. I didn't get into that sort of detail because I had one month to write my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, you've drawn on voluminous resources produced by the VJ, and some of those resources actually do quote figures for numbers of people believed to have been killed in the KLA, numbers of people killed in the VJ and the Serb MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. But again, if I was to get into a report that was describing how combat operations unfolded, what occurred during the operations, who initiated them, what weapons were used, where they took place and how long they lasted, that would require probably at least a year. Much of the documentation on that presumably hasn't been translated for a start. My Milosevic report took two years to write.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: See I don't want to spend anymore time on this point; I'm sure everybody will be relieved to hear that. But just to crystallise it, the whole point here is that you have in your report not given any indication that there are other radically different and on the face of it reliable opinions as to the size of the KLA at the time that we're all talking about. And that is a very important issue when we're looking at whether or not there is a command structure and what the nature of that structure, if any, would be. Do you not agree?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report scope was not to go into the structure of the KLA or the means and mechanisms of commanding the KLA. I identified some references in the documentation I reviewed that suggested that the KLA did have some semblance of a central structure and the ability to coordinate operations, but I didn't go into detail on its command structure. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Because you had no information on which to do so, did you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information was available. I didn't have the time nor the direction to look into that. I believe that information would be handled by other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that's a -- if not a convenient answer, a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The use of the word "moment" encourages me. How many more moments do you think there might be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I have some questioning of some moment to come. I would -- we will certainly finish within the next session. I will certainly finish within the next session. I would think probably three-quarters of an hour to one hour. I hope you won't hold me to that, but I will hope to hold myself to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. We will resume at 5 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yesterday, you may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, red light.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've entered the red light district again. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yesterday you may recall I asked you at page 76, line 1 of yesterday's transcript about Frenki's boys at the bottom of page 75 and the JSO. You gave this answer: "A. Sorry, it relates to Frenki Simatovic. Whether it's Frenki Simatovic of the JSO as I have put to you isn't clear. He has a role within the ministry, a department within the ministry. I'm not sure whether he was a member of the JSO or not. I'm don't think he was." Now, if you could take, please, the documents that were handed to you a little earlier that started with page 10084. You've got that group of documents, Coo 10084 it says on the first page. And in fact I want the last page of that set of documents which is document K022-7617. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: That I believe -- I think you can confirm was part of an appendix to the report that you provided for the Milosevic trial. Am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And do we see there the same Simatovic, Frenki, and under remarks: "Responsible for special units of the" -- I'm sorry, I'm looking at the wrong line. Under "Remarks," "Authority over the JSO." Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And is that your understanding -- does that at least refresh your memory now that Frenki Simatovic was indeed somebody who had responsibility for the JSO?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evidence suggests he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Your Honour, yesterday the question was whether or not this person was a member of the JSO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, the precise question was this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just carry on, Mr. Harvey, don't be distracted by profound statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'll try very hard not to rise to that bait.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, I said to you yesterday I would come back to the anti-terrorist units, and I want to do so quite briefly by reference to some testimony you yourself gave at page 10082 in Milosevic -- which I hope you have to hand. Is that there? That should be what you were given yesterday, not in today's bundle. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't seem to be in yesterday's. I've got 10084 and preceding that is 10038.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I see I've done it again. I apologise, but let me read this to you and see if it does help your refresh your recollection. It begins at the bottom of 10081. You had been asked about whether you came across irregularities at brigade level in army conduct and you gave this answer: "A. Irregularities concerning what actually happened on the ground were not within the general scope of the report. Where I came across information related to some of our indictment issues, that was put into the report and no conclusions were drawn from that by me or whether or not a crime" -- I'm sorry, "on whether or not a crime was committed." And this is the passage I want to focus on: "The closest I came to commenting or concluding of anything that might be a irregularity was the contents of a MUP report from 1998 where they -- it was an operations order where they specified that the attack should be made" -- sorry, "should make use of Chinese ammunition, which to me seemed strange, specifying the ammunition by origin in an operations order." Do you as you sit here today recall that testimony and recall the information that you had come across relating to an order that Chinese ammunition should be used?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that. The report was actually 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And having looked again, you have found a document which I think is 0302-8516 in translation, and again if I can read briefly from that, that was kindly provided to me by Mr. Nicholls after I raised this question. "On 29th January, 1999, the platoon leader and the squad leaders of PJP, special police units, together with the sector leader from the Celopek PO shall make a reconnaissance of the area and the ambush locations. The platoon leader of PJP shall provide grenade launchers and ammunition manufactured in China, while immediately prior to the execution of the task he shall inspect the forces and acquaint them with the plan and specific tasks." Say all of that to say. Chinese ammunition was generally associated at that time with the KLA. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And there was your reasonable conclusion that instructing a unit of the special forces of the MUP to use Chinese ammunition was an order to set up an ambush and a killing that could be used as black propaganda for blaming on the KLA?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall precisely how I phrased it. And I think I phrased it as a possibility rather than a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No, I'm not should going that you actually phrased it one way or the other, but I'm ask you as you sit here today: That is the reasonable inference, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's one inference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Okay. When we -- can I just ask you, as part of your job - and I did ask you yesterday how you do your job and what is basis is on which you do your research - you have told us, and I paraphrase, that part of your job is to look for evidence that can be used to bring indictments or support indictments that have already been brought. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So if you are going through evidence that you think may be helpful -- if you come across evidence that may be helpful in a particular case, you will take it to whoever the Prosecution team is handling that case and say, by the way, have you guys seen this, for example?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you ever come across evidence that a police team working with the SAJ who had been responsible for the massacre of the Jashari family were also involved in supplying Chinese weaponry and UKA -- sorry, UCK or KLA uniforms to, shall we say, nonconventional forces for use in assassinations?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall any information like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you never become aware of the witness given the protective identity pseudonym of K5 in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to see his testimony to be reminded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, I have copies of his witness statement which I'm happy to make available to you and the rest of the parties, and I don't wish to dwell lengthily on it. But perhaps if everyone could be shown that briefly, you can at least identify from the content whether it's something that you've come across before. Of course I do not know the identity of K5 and I don't know whether anybody else in court may be able to help you on that. Just very briefly, the date of the statement is the 27th of October, 2000, and in summary it concerns how this particular ethnic Albanian police informant was recruited and he gives very remarkable detail about how he was allegedly recruited by the chief of the Ferizaj police station to participate in bombings, grenade attacks, and killings that could later be blamed on the KLA and so that those killed by this unit could be defamed as spies. That's a very brief summary.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a vague recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You have a very vague recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Now, did -- does your vague recollection assist you as to whether before coming into court to testify yesterday you were aware that there was a witness who was held forward to this Tribunal, to another Trial Chamber of this Tribunal, as being a witness of truth for the Prosecution who maintained that the Serb police special forces were deliberately carrying out acts of this nature in order to discredit the KLA as early as March of 1998?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't information that I recalled when I was writing my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, when you were writing your report I asked you before you came in to testify yesterday. You have indicated just now that you have a vague recollection of this witness's testimony, at least of a statement that we have assigned 27th of October, the year 2000. What I'm asking you is: Did you have that vague recollection before you came into court yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You obviously have seen this statement at some time in the past. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A long time ago, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you know how long ago?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Before you wrote your report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Are you aware that this is a witness regarded by the Prosecution as a witness of truth?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume he is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And the acts undertaken by special forces of MUP and the attempts to discredit the KLA were not acts that you thought of as important to at least refer to in any way as you were compiling your report in order to attempt to assist this Tribunal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. As I explained earlier, Your Honours, the scope of my report was limited by the time available, and it wasn't within my ability in that time available to go into great depth in looking into how the operations were actually conducted. I reported from the limited sources that I consulted on what the responses to the crisis in Kosovo were by the Serb forces and what was seen by members of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I hear your answer. As an employee of the OTP, advising on the strength of evidence available for the bringing of indictments, can you offer any insight into why no single person has been indicted for the widespread and systemic attacks on the Kosovan Albanian population that occurred throughout 1998?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I wasn't involved in --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you. The only thing -- I've been reminded very helpfully by Mr. Khan. I'm very bad at housekeeping. And I have not asked to exhibit the documents that I have tendered to this witness in the course of yesterday and today. I do apologise for that. Subject to that, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, these were put in various passages to the witness. Is there anything more other than the passages that you put to him that is relevant to this trial and which we should accept?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: May I just take a moment to think about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can reflect on it as others are proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Right. That's what I was thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My first reaction is the use that was made of it by you displaces any need to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I see wise nodding going on around you. I'll consult. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to make it clear, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: No further questions on behalf of Mr. Musliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have no re-direct. I'll just point out that the document put to Mr. Coo yesterday by Mr. Harvey, 03078003, was not sought to make an exhibit. That is already included as annex B to the report, so that is in already. And in terms of the transcripts and excerpts, I do not believe that those should be admitted. I think the relevant parts were read out and we shouldn't be putting in transcripts of testimony in other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, having consulted and thought carefully about it, I think the only document, since it hasn't been looked at in detail but since it is one which this witness does recall having considered should simply be marked for identification, and that is the last one, the K5 statement. I'm not suggesting that it should go into evidence, but in order that we understand what we've been talking about, I would ask that that one be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be DB4, MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, you'll be pleased to know that with a flurry at the end, that has concluded the questions that will be asked of you. May we thank you for your assistance and you are now free to return to your other activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
