utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have three statements to put into evidence; they are agreed. The first two will be handled by Mr. Black and then I'll handle the last one. So I'll defer at this time to Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I think a small -- much-smaller-than-in-the-past packet is being distributed to you. The drill I would propose is the same as the one we have done before. These are two -- well, they are 92 bis materials for two witnesses. We have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. reached agreement with the Defence on both of them. And if it pleases Your Honour, I would move orally to add each of these witnesses to our witness list and to admit their evidence in written form pursuant to Rule 92 bis. I can do that one by one or however Your Honour prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There are no special measures in respect of either?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: There are no protective measures, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Since it is by agreement, both the statement -- well, first the statement of Francis Ledwidge will be admitted into evidence and his name will be added to the Prosecution witness list.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just hold a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P242.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the statement of Zoran Lesic will be admitted evidence and that name will be added to the witness list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P243.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's all from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I come with a much more sizeable bundle; it's this large notebook. It's the notebook of Witness L103.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And also by agreement we would ask that this witness's statement and the 17 tabs which are corresponding exhibits be admitted into evidence pursuant to 92 bis. There are a few wrinkles, though no serious ones, with respect to this bundle. Since we prepared the bundle we have actually managed to do the 92 bis procedure and we received the 92 bis statement just minutes before we started court today. And so what I would like to do is distribute that, the actual 92 bis statement, which is identical to the statement which is contained in the bundle and which has been previously disclosed. It's just 92 bis'd. And I have both the unredacted and the redacted version, and I will come to that issue later. But if this could be distributed. Now, just to be clear with respect to this statement and the attached exhibits, we provided a spreadsheet which is the first page of the binder, and this spreadsheet explains the correspondence between the tabs -- the exhibits at each tab and the paragraphs in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The -- the only difficulty is that these paragraph numbers correspond to the statement that was not 92 bis'd. The 92 bis procedure changed the numbering of the paragraphs. So what I would propose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you're going to let us have a substitute sometime in the future?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, yes, that is what I would propose that we will allowed to substitute a new chart just for the assistance of the Court and the parties that will show the correspondence between the paragraph numbers of the statement and the tabs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We would also ask that the -- for protective measures for the name and identifying information of the witness; this has been agreed by Defence counsel. The witness is a still-serving member of the Serbian State Security and therefore has concerns about security and safety. And therefore we would ask simply that the name and identifying information of the witness be redacted. In addition, in paragraph 25 of the 92 bis version of the statement there's a reference to a name of a witness, and therefore we would ask that that be redacted from the public version. And also corresponding tab 5, the exhibit at tab 5, will also have to be under seal. So what I would propose is that the unredacted version of the statement and all of the exhibits go into evidence under seal and that we then prepare a separate version with the name of the witness redacted, the witness himself, plus the references to the other witness redacted and tab 5 taken out, and that would become the public version of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, this is getting a bit complicated. This witness is on your list, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He is on our list, though not by name, just by description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: By description. By consent --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm sorry to interrupt. There is one matter that I neglected to raise and it was important to the Defence and I want to say it before the Court because it goes to the consent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In paragraph 15 of the original statement and it's now paragraph 21 of the 92 bis statement there is a statement which is arguably ambiguous because the witness says in that paragraph -- he says: "I have been shown a series of documents and I can confirm that all of the documents shown to me are copies of the same documents seized by the MUP in Lapusnik on 25 July 1998 which I referred to and listed in my -- in the report." The Prosecution's understanding of that - and it will be clear in context - is that the only knowledge that the witness has is what was told to him when the documents were provided to him, and they were represented to him as having been seized by the MUP on that date in Lapusnik. And that is explained in other paragraphs of the statement. And it is our -- our understanding is that that is the extent of his information when he says: "I can confirm that these -- these are the documents seized by the MUP," he is referring to what was represented to him. That is our understanding of that statement; that is how we intend to rely on it. And it is on that basis that Defence counsel were agreeable to this statement going into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very grateful to my learned friend for clarifying. For the record, we agreed to the statement with two caveats. In relation to paragraph 14 - again, it follows logically from what was accepted and the Prosecution's understanding of paragraph 15 - paragraph 14, the basis upon which it is accepted is where the witness states that "because the documents seized were in Albanian," and our understanding - and we're willing to accept it on the basis that it should read in fact, that Your Honours should read it, that "the documents handed over to me by the MUP were in Albanian." And similarly paragraph 15 should be read as, in our submission and with the agreement I understand of my learned friend for the Prosecution should read as: "Documents shown to me are copies provided to me by MUP." Of course he cannot state that they were the documents seized actually in Lapusnik. He doesn't give any evidence at all as to provenance. And upon that basis we are happy for the evidence to be put in in the manner that my learned friend seeks to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. We can't of course by consent amend a statement, but I have endorsed the side the copy here with the notation that in each case the word "seized" in paragraphs 20 and 21, as they now are, should be read as "handed to me by MUP."

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that will meet the agreed understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Most definitely. That works perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, just to be clear, these documents, when they were handed to the witness were represented as having being seized, and that is part of his statement. But otherwise that is agreeable, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, this is probably me misreading, but when I look at the statement it seems we have two paras 21. Maybe that could be clarified. Or am I just off the chart here? And also I think there are others paras that have double numbering.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was pointed out to me a just few moments ago, that the paragraph numbering has restarted. And I'm not sure how we are going to handle that. Perhaps what we will have to do with consent is renumber the paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: That seems to be safe otherwise we have built-in ambiguity here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It creates confusion. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that appears to occur in what I understand is no longer the statement to be relied upon. We've been given the Rule 92 bis-compliant statement now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, in fact, it is the one. It is the 92 bis statement that that occurs in. And I apologise for that misnumbering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I don't have a misnumbered copy then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: You drew the lucky one then, obviously. That's even worse, we have several versions now; that's even worse than the first observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's very strange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Maybe you could align it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That is something that I think we can have corrected by tomorrow. I can state this, that the substance of the statements are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It concerns me that the Chamber has two separate versions of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that concerns me as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would say, Mr. Whiting, that it would be unwise to receive a document even though it doesn't have any duplication of paragraph numbering until you can check what it is that has happened that has given us two distinct forms of what is apparently the same document, because we cannot be confident that either one is the one we should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, and I don't know how the Court wishes to proceed. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would suggest -- I'm sorry to give you administrative work, which we normally seek to avoid but as I understand it there will be no further need for us to sit after today in the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. JUDGE PARKER. Could I suggest that you have leave to files a written motion with the right exhibits after the close of the Prosecution case and with the right papers in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. We can certainly do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And on the basis that the attitude of the Defence will remain unchanged, it will then be accepted and given a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I apologise for the confusion. This all happened very quickly at the last minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, yes. Very well. And we might even reserve there number P244 for it. Who knows?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, is there anything further, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. The only thing further, Your Honour, before the Prosecution says the magic words, is Mr. Black yesterday noted that we were still waiting for the ICMP report for Fehmi Xhema, aka Tafa. And we would ask, and I believe this has been agreed to by the Defence, that we be permitted after the close of the Prosecution case that we put that document in once it becomes available. The substance of the document has been already described to the Court and to the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Leave will be granted to the Prosecution to file motions for the admission of the two documents that have just been identified. One of them is incorrectly described as a document; it's many documents. That's one that is foreshadowed to be P244. And the other is the report which Mr. Black mentioned -- I'm not sure when it was but recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With that then, the Prosecution rests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Are there any motions at this stage by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: On behalf of Fatmir Limaj, there are no motions at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On behalf of Haradin Bala, at this point in time there are no motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, similarly, on behalf of Isak Musliu, there are no motions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The anticipation of the Chamber is that it would not be immediately convenient to proceed with Defence evidence. Further, it will be necessary, given the Rules, for the Defence to give notice of various things to the Prosecution before commencing the case for the Defence, if I can put it in the singular, although it is three distinct defences. That therefore will require that there be some time before we resume evidence. Could I have an indication, perhaps, Mr. Mansfield, what time you think would be appropriate?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. May I indicate we have had extensive discussions between all counsel, including those representing the Prosecution, to try and arrive at a reasonable assessment of what is required to allow both the Prosecution to analyse what we will give notice of. May I put forward a suggested time and that is that there be an interval of three weeks from next Monday, totaling all together three and a half weeks if one includes what is left of this week, which would take us, if Your Honours were to permit that interval of time, would take us into May plainly and would result in the Defence being in a position, subject to any other difficulties, on Monday, May the 9th. And so far -- I just pause for a moment so that you may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: -- see where that date falls. There are a number of reasons. I can elaborate in detail if needed, but I can give an indication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps to break it up a little, Mr. Mansfield, can you tell me when it is or by what period you, at least, for your client would be in a position to provide a list of witnesses and a list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. The -- what I was going to indicate to Your Honour was that there is a projected visit to Kosovo for reasons I can't go into, but that visit will take place as soon as possible and certainly by the end of next week it will have been completed. And what I've indicated to the Prosecution on a much earlier date than today was that it would be helpful for us to be allowed that period of time to finalise the list, for example, of witnesses. But it would mean that by the Monday of the following week we would be in a position to proffer a list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that Monday, the 2nd of May, or the 25th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, it would be -- I was contemplating the week of the 25th of May [sic]. The reason why I'm contemplating an earlier date is the Prosecution themselves have indicated they need certainly two, but preferably three weeks to have a look at what we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the 25th gives you time enough including the visit that you're contemplating to prepare lists and to file and serve. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, because the other thing -- if I can shoot forward a moment -- the reason why we're trying to work towards certain dates and a relatively, if I may put it this way, tight schedule is we're conscious of the summer break and we're attempting to marshal defence evidence starting at that date in May that will enable a certain amount of time for each of the Defence cases. So, for example, with relation to Fatmir Limaj's case, we're estimating it to be not less than two weeks, but probably three weeks in length, total. And that the cases that follow -- well, I leave to others to speak for themselves possibly, but we've tried to estimate those as well, encompassing certainly a further three weeks on top of that for the other cases. Because some of the witnesses that I will be calling will obviously impinge on other cases so that it won't be necessary for them to be called twice, plainly. And plainly there will be other witnesses that will not require being called live as well so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Defence may make use of 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: So I hope that's the best estimate I can give. Plainly, I also undertook with the Prosecution that if we're in a position to provide -- which we almost certainly will be -- some are obvious witnesses before the expiry of that period of time in Kosovo, then we'll do so. So we will do it as soon as we can do it within that time. But there is a need, I'm afraid, for a visit to Kosovo in order to finalise matters with some potential witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Could I ask, the estimate you gave for your client's case --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- that included reasonable provision for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Examination by other --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, it was allowing for that. So, by example, so Your Honour may get the measure of it, we certainly anticipate that the defendant that I represent, Fatmir Limaj, would be in the witness box, both answering questions from me and the Prosecution and possibly others for at least a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: But it could be more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I see -- I'm not sure whether Mr. Whiting's raising his eyebrows because it's too long or too short. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very difficult for you to estimate cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- for that particular --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: But as you will see, we have made an attempt to allow at least a session for Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you're generosity continues, Mr. Mansfield. Thank you very much for that. Do you have anything, Mr. Guy-Smith, to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If it's of any assistance to the Trial Chamber, we contemplate that the case for Mr. Bala will take somewhere between a week to two at the absolute maximum. Probably closer to a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And we do not expect any cross-examination from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're optimism continues. I'm afraid that Chamber has to be more pessimistic. Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Musliu it is anticipated that the Defence case could last between two to three weeks, and I would endorse what Mr. Mansfield has said about the start date of the Defence portion of the case, namely on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly we have no quarrel with the proposed start date. We would only ask that the Defence comply with the requirements of Rule 65 ter (G) no later than the 25th of April. I couldn't remember what month we were in. Giving us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, we're still in April. Giving us two weeks then after that date before the start of the Defence case. And it sounded to me like there would be no difficulty with counsel complying with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Perhaps I should say in relation to that, given that Mr. Musliu's case will start last, after both Mr. Limaj and Mr. Bala's cases have been heard by the Trial Chamber, there's perhaps not the same degree of urgency for the Defence to file the 65 ter (G) summaries with the Prosecution on the 25th of April. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's called creeping compliance with Rule 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I can say it's hoped that the representatives of Mr. Musliu's team will be in Kosovo next week and it's hoped that it would take no more than one week after that to finalise the list -- to be able to provide the Prosecution with it and of course the Trial Chamber with it on the 30th of April with it at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Looking at what is proposed by counsel and conscious that there is at least one day just following the date you propose, which is a holiday observed by the Tribunal, a festival date, the 16th of May; and conscious from the experience that we have had here of the difficulties which appear greater for Defence than for Prosecution in organising a flow of witnesses, may the Chamber put out the radical proposition that the Defence cases might commence a week later than you propose? Is that going to be something that will assist? That would be Tuesday, the 17th, because the 16th is a holiday. On the basis then that there should be adequate time to comply with Rule 65 ter in all its elements by all parties for the Defence, and the Prosecution can unmistakably make their inquiries so that we won't have the false starts that seem to bedevil so many things here of a nominal start and people calling for adjournments because they haven't got quite everything organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can say on behalf of Mr. Musliu that that would work for the Musliu Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're in descending order or ascending order, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think it's a lovely idea, and I fully endorse your radical suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm certainly fully in support of that. If I may then, on that basis -- so I'm just checking the dates. It would assist us if we could then -- this is the creeping aspect of this of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh dear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: We have given a commitment for the 25th. If we could creep into that week, that will help us, because we are supposed to be here that week consulting with Mr. Limaj so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What about the Wednesday, the 27th --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, that would help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which ran from today. Close of business, 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, the date is certainly fine for the Prosecution. We have been alerted via e-mail by the Witnesses Unit that getting a witness here on the date after a UN holiday could prove difficult. I don't know who the first witness will be, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand it will be the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I didn't understand that it would the accused who would be the first witness. I assumed he'd be the last witness. That's fine. Well, I guess he'll be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's an American habit we don't have. Counsel will appreciate that the absence of a need for the Chamber to spend time on other motions at this point has had a significant influence on our ability to make a little more time available than would otherwise would have been possible. So we thank you for that. Very well. The time fixed for compliance by all Defences with Rule 65 ter is when -- the close of business, Wednesday, the 27th of April. And we will resume on Tuesday, the 17th of May. I'm afraid I can't tell you whether that will be morning or afternoon because the planning of court sittings hasn't reached that point, but it will be one or the other. In this case -- well, sorry, really aside from this case but relevant to all counsel here is the application which the Chamber has received to make available certain information to those engaged in the Milosevic trial. I raise it to inquire whether there is any submission which Defence counsel wish to make in respect of that motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, the Prosecution will be able to give the Chamber its position in the course of the next -- overnight?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we filed a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You did, but there is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- question of whether you had considered disclosure of --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- the identities of certain witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and on that matter we can provide something to the Court by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would be of importance to the other trial to get that order out tomorrow. There is outstanding a decision by this Chamber in this trial about the admission or the purposes of admission of two statements. A decision is imminent. So that will be known to you, I would expect, and known before it is necessary to comply with Rule 65 ter, should there be any cross-relevance between the two. I don't know whether the Defence contemplates any expert witnesses. I just am conscious that under Rule 94 bis there's a 30-day time which the Prosecution may require after having notice of it. So if counsel could keep that in mind if there's any expert evidence looming you'll need to give early notice of that to avoid a delay of the process. Does any counsel see need for a Rule 73 ter pre-Defence conference? Can I say that counsel -- the Chamber has the view that given the general experience of counsel and the management of the case to date, that there would not appear to be any need for anything other than the most formal conference, which could even occur on the morning of the 17th of May immediately before the commencement of the case. But if there is thought by counsel to be need for it, well the Chamber will of course be available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you for the offer. I think there is no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't see a need, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Orders. At the moment the Chamber see need to be making any orders about the length of the Defence case or the number of witnesses or who they are to be called for the reason I mentioned a few moments ago. In other words, we're confident that we can leave such matters in the hands of counsel. And if our confidence becomes shattered, we will not fail to act. There seems to be no other matter that needs to be mentioned. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: There's one. I wonder if I might just mention one matter, and that is to ask if you have any idea when it might be possible to receive your ruling in relation to prior statements that has been -- because it may be of relevance obviously to the Defence case, and I think if there's a possibility it may arise at the start of the Defence case and it would be of interest to us to know. If there isn't any indication, then I obviously don't take it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I indicated, it can be expected very shortly, Mr. Mansfield. The production processes are likely to make it early next week rather than tomorrow or Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, I'm very grateful for that indication. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There was one evidentiary matter that we never finished having a conversation about; it concerned a document that Mr. Black had sought to introduce. I am at this point satisfied with the state of the record and I am withdrawing any further concerns but wanted to make sure that the house was tidy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for that piece of housekeeping because it slipped under my guard. I had not had my mind to it, but my brother Thelin, nodded knowingly so he would not have let me forget it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have noted that between the three of you the amount of detail that goes unnoticed is not much, if at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You flatter the two that sit with me. We now adjourn and resume sitting on Tuesday, the 17th of next month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of May, 2005 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
